meaning: Lists two (or more) things of the same kind: “whether A or B”, “A or B, either is fine”. With a negative, it means “neither A nor B”.
connection: Noun + でも + noun + でも (verbs and い-adjectives use 「〜ても〜ても」)

senses.label: Whether A or B
senses.meaning: Gives two examples of the same kind and says the result is the same either way: “whether A or B, ...”. Usually followed by a positive statement such as 「大丈夫だ」 or 「できる」.
senses.connection: Noun + でも + noun + でも + positive statement
examples: I can eat both meat and fish.
Rain or snow, the game will go ahead.
It's a game that both kids and adults can enjoy.

senses.label: A or B, either is fine
senses.meaning: Offers a few options and says any of them is fine. It sounds relaxed and considerate. Often followed by 「いい」, 「かまわない」, or 「どうぞ」.
senses.connection: Noun + でも + noun + でも (いい／かまわない／どうぞ)
examples: Coffee or tea, please have whichever you like.
Phone or email is fine, so please get in touch.

senses.label: Neither A nor B
senses.meaning: With a negative, 「〜でもない／〜でもありません」, it means “neither A nor B”. Often used for an in-between state or a noncommittal attitude.
senses.connection: Noun / な-adjective stem + でも + noun / な-adjective stem + でもない
examples: I neither like it nor dislike it.
He's neither a friend nor a boyfriend.

senses.label: No matter what you do
senses.meaning: Verbs and い-adjectives use 「〜ても〜ても」. It can pair two opposite actions (「押しても引いても」) or repeat the same word (「食べても食べても」). It stresses “no matter how much ...”, and is often followed by a negative or unexpected result.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も + verb te-form + も / い-adjective く + ても + い-adjective く + ても
examples: Push or pull, the door won't open.
No matter how much I eat, I don't gain weight.
Hot or cold, I go running every morning.

notes: It must come in pairs (or three or more): 「日本でも中国でもアメリカでも」. A single 「でも」 means “for example” or “even”, which is a different pattern.
The end of the sentence decides the meaning: 「AでもBでもいい」 is “either is fine”; 「AでもBでもない」 is “neither”.
It is often wrapped up with 「何でも」 or 「どちらでも」: 「肉でも魚でも、何でも食べます」.
Nouns and な-adjectives take 「でも」; verbs and い-adjectives take 「ても」 (verbs with the ん sound change take 「でも」, as in 「読んでも」).

daily.title: A friend visiting your home
daily.description: Using 「AでもBでも」 when letting a friend pick a drink sounds easygoing.
daily.example: Tea or juice, drink whatever you like.

daily.title: Setting a time to meet
daily.description: Telling a friend any day works for you.
daily.example: Saturday or Sunday, either is fine with me.

daily.title: Praising a child who isn't picky
daily.description: A parent describes their child's eating habits.
daily.example: Vegetables, meat, this kid eats everything.

work.title: Customer service contact options
work.description: A company tells customers on its website or by phone that they can get in touch in several ways.
work.example: We accept questions by phone or email.

work.title: Announcing the meeting format
work.description: The organizer explains to colleagues how they can attend.
work.example: You can join the meeting in person or online.

etymology: 「でも」 comes from 「で」, the connective form of the copula 「だ」, plus the particle 「も」. It originally meant “even if it is ...”. Used in pairs, “even if it's A, even if it's B” came to mean “whether A or B”. 「ても」 is the particle 「て」 + 「も」.

similar.title: 〜でも (question word + でも)
similar.explanation: 「何でも」 and 「誰でも」 cover everything with one question word; 「AでもBでも」 names specific examples. They often go together: 「肉でも魚でも、何でも食べます」.

similar.title: 〜も〜も
similar.explanation: 「AもBも」 simply means “both A and B” (「肉も魚も好きだ」). 「AでもBでも」 has a concessive feel: “whether it's A or B, ...”.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, “whether A or B”, but 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 is written and stiff (N2). 「〜でも〜でも」 is everyday speech.

meaning: Presents a view widely held by society or experts: “it is believed that ...”, “it is thought that ...”. Objective in tone.
connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjectives may take だ) + と考えられている

senses.label: It is believed that
senses.meaning: A view is generally accepted by society or by experts. It is not the speaker's personal opinion but an objective statement. Common in news, textbooks, and explanations.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form, or noun / な-adjective + だ, + と考えられている (polite: と考えられています)
examples: Lack of sleep is believed to be one of the causes of illness.
It is believed that there was once a large town in this area.
Laughing is thought to be good for your health.

senses.label: It used to be believed
senses.meaning: The past 「〜と考えられていた」 means people used to think so. It often implies the view has since changed. Often used with 「昔は」 or 「かつては」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と考えられていた
examples: In the past, the Earth was believed to be the center of the universe.
This disease was once thought to be incurable.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜と考えられている + noun」 describes a noun: “the ... that is believed to be ...”. Very common in news reports.
senses.connection: Plain form + と考えられている + noun
examples: The police are examining the part believed to have caused the accident.
There is a tree that is thought to be the oldest in the world.

notes: 「考えられる」 is the passive of 「考える」. 「〜と考えられている」 stresses that the view is widely accepted.
The subject is unspecified “people” or “experts” and is usually left out. Don't use it for your own opinion: ✕「私は〜と考えられている」; say 「私は〜と思う」.
More grounded and objective than 「〜と言われている」. Common in science, academic writing, and the news.
Formal writing often links to the next clause with 「〜と考えられており、」. In speech you may hear 「〜って考えられてる」.

daily.title: After a science show
daily.description: Telling a friend something you learned on TV.
daily.example: Apparently birds are thought to be descendants of dinosaurs.

daily.title: At a museum
daily.description: A guide or a display panel introduces an artifact to visitors.
daily.example: This pottery is believed to have been made about 5,000 years ago.

daily.title: Talking health with family
daily.description: Quoting a common view to get a family member to eat breakfast.
daily.example: Skipping breakfast is thought to be bad for you, you know.

work.title: News report
work.description: An announcer uses objective wording to report the cause of an incident.
work.example: The cause of the fire is believed to be a cigarette.

work.title: Academic presentation
work.description: A researcher presents the accepted theory in a paper or talk.
work.example: Rising temperatures are thought to be related to this phenomenon.

etymology: The passive 「考えられる」 of 「考える」 plus 「ている」 for an ongoing state. 「と」 is the quotation particle marking the content. Literally “is being thought (by people)”, meaning the view exists as common wisdom.

similar.title: 〜と言われている
similar.explanation: 「〜と言われている」 means “it is said that”, and can cover legends and sayings. 「〜と考えられている」 stresses a reasoned view with some basis, so it sounds more objective and academic.

similar.title: 〜とされている
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, but 「〜とされている」 is more written and formal, and can also mean “is defined as” by a rule. 「〜と考えられている」 also works in speech.

similar.title: 〜と考えられる
similar.explanation: 「〜と考えられる」 usually shows the speaker's own inference: “it can be assumed that”. Adding 「ている」 shows the view is already widely held.

similar.title: 〜と思っている
similar.explanation: 「〜と思っている」 is the thought of a specific person (someone else or yourself). With 「〜と考えられている」, the thinker is people in general.

meaning: Written style. A claim is widely accepted, or something is set that way by a rule: “is considered ...”, “is said to ...”, “is defined as ...”.
connection: Plain form / noun + とされている

senses.label: Is considered / is said to
senses.meaning: A claim is widely accepted by society, scholars, or tradition. More written and formal than 「〜と考えられている」. Common in history, legends, and scientific explanations.
senses.connection: Plain form (nouns attach directly) + とされている／とされています
examples: This temple is said to have been built in the 8th century.
Green tea is considered good for your health.
This shrine is said to bring luck in finding love.

senses.label: Is set as / is defined as
senses.meaning: Something is set or regarded that way by law, rules, or custom: “is set as”, “is regarded as”. Common in laws, regulations, and manuals.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + とされている (often 「〜ものとされている」, 「〜ことが望ましいとされている」)
examples: The application deadline is set for the end of March.
During meetings, it is advised to turn off your mobile phone.

senses.label: Was once considered
senses.meaning: 「〜とされていた」 shows a past accepted view. It often implies it was later overturned or revised.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + とされていた
examples: For a long time, this painting was considered the work of a different artist.

notes: 「される」 is the passive of 「する」. 「〜とされている」 is written style; in everyday conversation people say 「〜と言われている」 or 「〜って言われてる」.
Nouns attach directly without 「だ」: 「国宝とされている」.
News and academic writing often link to the next clause with 「〜とされており、」.
It means basically the same as N1 「〜とされる」; the 「ている」 form stresses that the view or rule is still in effect.

daily.title: Reading a travel guide
daily.description: A guidebook introduces a famous spot.
daily.example: This hot spring is said to be good for stiff shoulders.

daily.title: Health news
daily.description: TV or online news introduces a general health guideline.
daily.example: About seven hours of sleep a day is considered ideal.

work.title: Reading terms of service
work.description: A contract or terms explain when you are deemed to have agreed.
work.example: By using this service, you are deemed to have agreed to the terms.

work.title: Reporting an accident
work.description: A reporter relays the officially announced cause.
work.example: The cause of the accident is said to be the driver's carelessness.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A researcher describes the status of an existing theory.
work.example: This theory is now considered incorrect.

etymology: 「する」 can mean “to treat as” or “to regard as” (「AをBとする」 = to set A as B). Its passive 「される」 + 「ている」 gives 「AはBとされている」 = “A is regarded as B”. From there come the meanings “is considered”, “is said to”, and “is defined as”.

similar.title: 〜とされる
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, and both are written style. 「〜とされる」 is common in headlines and definitions; 「〜とされている」 stresses that the view or rule is still in effect.

similar.title: 〜と考えられている
similar.explanation: 「〜と考えられている」 focuses on a view people reached by reasoning, and works in speech too. 「〜とされている」 is more formal and can also mean “is defined as” by a rule.

similar.title: 〜と言われている
similar.explanation: 「〜と言われている」 means “it is said”, common in both speech and writing, and can cover legends and sayings. 「〜とされている」 is more formal and sounds more like an established view.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: For rules, 「〜ことになっている」 is the spoken “the rule is that ...”; 「〜とされている」 is the written form used in official documents and laws.

title: 〜ら (plural)
meaning: Added to personal pronouns, demonstratives, or nouns for people to make them plural: “-s”, “these”, “... and others”. More casual than 「たち」, or more formal in writing.
connection: Personal pronoun / 「これ・それ・あれ」 / noun for people + ら

senses.label: Plural pronouns
senses.meaning: Added to 「彼」, 「僕」, 「君」, 「俺」, 「お前」, 「あいつ」, etc. to mean “they”, “we”, “you (plural)”. 「彼ら」 is a common neutral word. 「僕ら」, 「俺ら」, and 「お前ら」 are casual and not used toward superiors.
senses.connection: 彼ら／僕ら／君ら／俺ら／お前ら／あいつら／我ら
examples: They're coming to Japan next week.
We always go home together.
You guys, be quiet!

senses.label: Plural demonstratives
senses.meaning: 「これら」, 「それら」, 「あれら」 mean “these” or “those (things)”. They are written style; in conversation people usually say 「これ」 or 「こういうもの」.
senses.connection: これら／それら／あれら (+ の + noun)
examples: We'll use these materials at the meeting.
We discussed those issues.

senses.label: ... and others
senses.meaning: Added to names or nouns for people, such as job titles, to mean “... and others” or “... and colleagues”. Common in news and official documents, with an objective tone. Also used in words like 「子どもら」.
senses.connection: Name + さん／氏／教授 + ら; 選手ら／学生ら／子どもら
examples: A research team led by Professor Yamada developed a new drug.
The athletes returned home with smiles on their faces.
Children are playing in the park.

notes: 「ら」 is more casual than 「たち」. Don't use 「〜ら」 for superiors or elders (✕「先生ら」); use the honorific plural 「〜方（がた）」: 「先生方」.
「彼ら」 and 「これら」 are neutral words, common in writing too, and not rude.
In the news, 「Aさんら」 means “A and others”, with A as the representative. The others aren't necessarily the same kind of person.
Don't confuse it with 「〜らしい」: 「彼らしい」 means “typical of him”, not a plural.

daily.title: Inviting a friend out
daily.example: We're going to karaoke tomorrow. Wanna come?

daily.title: Talking about other people
daily.description: Telling family or friends where some people went.

daily.title: Hearing it on the news
daily.description: TV news often uses 「〜ら」 for “... and others”.
daily.example: Mr. Tanaka and others founded a new company.

work.title: Asking for confirmation in writing
work.description: Asking someone in an email or document to check a few points.

work.title: Research report
work.description: Citing someone else's research in a paper or report.
work.example: According to a survey by Professor Suzuki and colleagues, the number of users is rising every year.

etymology: 「ら」 is written with the kanji 「等」. In old Japanese it was already a suffix for plurals or “and so on”, as in 「子ら」 and 「我ら」. It is generally thought to have originally carried a humble or slightly dismissive nuance, which is why it still sounds more casual than 「たち」.

similar.title: 〜たち
similar.explanation: 「たち」 is the most common plural, neutral in politeness (「子どもたち」, 「私たち」). 「ら」 is more casual, or used in writing and the news. 「これら」 can't become ✕「これたち」.

similar.title: 〜ども
similar.explanation: 「ども」 is used for humility (「私ども」 = our company) or contempt (「野郎ども」). It carries stronger feeling than 「ら」.

similar.title: 〜方（がた）
similar.explanation: 「方」 is the honorific plural: 「先生方」, 「あなた方」. Don't use 「ら」 for people you should show respect to.
